My [LFX Linux Kernel Bug Fixing Mentorship](https://wiki.linuxfoundation.org/lkmp)
with Shuah Khan has ended. My [main write-up](../2026-10-26-sx93xx-fixes/index.qmd)
and my final report are with Shuah, so I am leaving that post as it is, at fifteen
applied patches. I am still sending patches, though, and some of them were already on
the mailing list when the mentorship ended. This post picks up from there. Each time a
patch is applied, I will add a section about it, a row in the [results table](#results)
and a bar in the timeline.

The first one is in a network driver rather than IIO. It also taught me something that
none of my IIO patches did: a correct fix can still be the wrong kind of fix for the
tree you send it to.

*First published on 13 November 2026 with the `vmxnet3` fix. Updated on 17 November
2026 with an ALSA fix for my own laptop.*

## vmxnet3: a DMA mapping of memory that can't be mapped

`vmxnet3` is the driver for VMware's paravirtual network card, the one most Linux
virtual machines on ESXi use. syzbot, Google's kernel fuzzer, reported a warning from
it while it was running with page allocation fault injection:

```
rejecting DMA map of vmalloc memory
```

The cause is in `vmxnet3_probe_device()`. The driver keeps its state in
`struct vmxnet3_adapter`, which is the private area of the `net_device`.
`alloc_netdev_mqs()` allocates that area with `kvzalloc()`. That function first tries
for physically contiguous memory, and if that fails it falls back to `vmalloc()`. The
adapter embeds 32 transmit and 32 receive queues, so it is well over a page, and a
large contiguous allocation is exactly the kind that fails under memory pressure, or
under fault injection.

The driver then mapped the whole adapter for DMA:

```c
	adapter->adapter_pa = dma_map_single(&adapter->pdev->dev, adapter,
					     sizeof(struct vmxnet3_adapter),
					     DMA_TO_DEVICE);
	if (dma_mapping_error(&adapter->pdev->dev, adapter->adapter_pa)) {
		dev_err(&pdev->dev, "Failed to map dma\n");
		err = -EFAULT;
		goto err_set_mask;
	}
```

`dma_map_single()` only works on memory that is physically contiguous, so when the
adapter is in vmalloc memory it warns and returns an error. Probe then fails, and the
VM has no network card.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-vmxnet3
%%| fig-cap: "Where the adapter's memory comes from, and what probe did with it. Only the vmalloc fallback triggered the bug."
flowchart TD
    A["alloc_netdev_mqs()"] --> B["kvzalloc(): contiguous allocation"]
    B -- succeeds --> C[adapter in contiguous memory]
    B -- fails --> D["vmalloc() fallback"]
    C --> E["dma_map_single(adapter)"]
    D --> F["dma_map_single(adapter)"]
    E --> G[probe continues]
    F --> H["before: WARNING, probe fails with -EFAULT<br/>after: nothing is mapped, probe continues"]
```

### What was the mapping for?

Before deleting anything, I needed to know what the device did with this address. It
goes into the area the driver shares with the virtual device, as the "driver data":

```c
	devRead->misc.ddPA = cpu_to_le64(adapter->adapter_pa);
	devRead->misc.ddLen = cpu_to_le32(sizeof(struct vmxnet3_adapter));
```

Three things suggested the device doesn't need it:

- **The same driver already opts out elsewhere.** Every per-queue descriptor in
  `vmxnet3` reports "no driver data" with `ddPA = ~0ULL` and `ddLen = 0`.
- **Other drivers for the same device never set it.** The vmxnet3 driver in DPDK
  leaves `misc.ddPA` alone entirely.
- **The device couldn't use it anyway.** The adapter is full of kernel pointers and
  locks. A hypervisor has no meaningful way to interpret a copy of it.

So the fix removes the mapping and reports no driver data in the shared area, in
the same way the queues already do:

```diff
-	devRead->misc.ddPA = cpu_to_le64(adapter->adapter_pa);
-	devRead->misc.ddLen = cpu_to_le32(sizeof(struct vmxnet3_adapter));
+	devRead->misc.ddPA = cpu_to_le64(~0ULL);
+	devRead->misc.ddLen = cpu_to_le32(0);
```

The rest of the patch is deletion: the `dma_map_single()` call, its error path, the
two `dma_unmap_single()` calls in the probe error path and in remove, and the
`adapter_pa` field. In total it is 3 lines added and 17 removed, and probe loses a way
to fail.

### Testing it without VMware

I don't have an ESXi host, but QEMU emulates a vmxnet3 card (`-device vmxnet3`), and
the kernel has `fail_page_alloc` to make page allocations fail on demand. I built a
kernel with KASAN and `CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG`, and tested three things before and after
the patch:

| Test | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| syzbot's C reproducer | WARNING, probe fails with `-EFAULT` | No warning |
| QEMU's emulated vmxnet3, normal boot | Probes, link up, ping works | Same |
| Unbind and rebind the NIC with order ≥ 4 allocations failing | WARNING, probe fails, the NIC is gone | Binds, ping works |

: How I tested the vmxnet3 fix in QEMU. {#tbl-vmxnet3-tests}

The third row is the one that matters. It is the real-world version of syzbot's
report: a VM under memory pressure that reloads the driver and loses its network.
I listed all of this under the `---` line and added "Not tested on ESXi".

### Review: "this does not seem like a real fix"

Simon Horman reviewed v1 four days later and gave it a `Reviewed-by:` with no
changes. A few hours later Jakub Kicinski, one of the networking maintainers, replied:

> Sounds fair but this does not seem like a real fix.
> If nobody complained about this failure mode for 13 years
> chances are we break more than we fix here.
>
> Please repost this for net-next in a couple of weeks without
> a Fixes tag.
>
> Also please remove the "never synced" stuff. That's purely
> relevant for intentionally hamstrung kernels. This is virt,
> there's no DMA to sync other than swiotlb.

followed by `pw-bot: defer`, which tells the netdev patchwork bot to set the patch
aside.

Neither point was about whether the code was right. They were about where it belonged.

**`net` versus `net-next`.** I had sent v1 to `net`, the tree for fixes that go to
Linus during the current release cycle and then to stable kernels, and I had added a
`Fixes:` tag pointing at the 2013 commit that introduced the mapping. Jakub's point was
that this is not how a maintainer measures a bug. The failure needs fault injection or
serious memory pressure, nobody had reported it in thirteen years, and the patch
changes what the driver tells a hypervisor I could not test against. Backporting that
to every stable kernel risks more than it fixes. As a cleanup in `net-next`, it gets a
full release cycle of testing first. When he deferred it, `net-next` was closed for the
merge window, so "a couple of weeks" meant waiting for it to reopen.

**"Never synced".** My commit message argued that the driver data was useless because
the mapping was `DMA_TO_DEVICE`, made once and never synced, so the device could only
ever see a stale copy. That sounded convincing to me, but Jakub pointed out that it
doesn't apply here. A virtual device reads guest memory directly, so syncing only
matters with a bounce buffer such as swiotlb. The argument would have been true for
real hardware, but it was wrong for this driver. The other reasons, the per-queue
descriptors and DPDK, were enough on their own, so v2 drops that sentence.

v2 had the same code. It targets `net-next`, has no `Fixes:` tag, drops the sync
argument and carries Simon's `Reviewed-by:`. I sent it the day after `net-next`
reopened, and Jakub applied it two days later.

## ALSA: my laptop was matched as a Legion

The second patch came from my own laptop, a Lenovo V14 G2 ITL. While I was looking at
why its speakers sound thin, I noticed this line in `dmesg`:

```
ALC257: picked fixup  for codec SSID 17aa:38b7
```

A "fixup" in the HD-audio driver is a machine-specific tweak: pin configurations,
amplifier setup, LED handling and so on. The driver picks one by looking up the
machine's IDs in a long table of quirks. There are two IDs to look at: the PCI
subsystem ID of the audio controller, and the subsystem ID the audio codec itself
reports. On most machines they are the same. On mine they are not:

| ID | Value |
|---|---|
| PCI subsystem ID (controller) | `17aa:380e` |
| Codec subsystem ID (ALC257) | `17aa:38b7` |

: The two IDs the driver can match on, for the V14 G2 ITL. {#tbl-alsa-ids}

### How the lookup goes wrong

`snd_hda_pick_fixup()` tries the PCI ID first. Nothing in the table matches
`17aa:380e`, so it falls back to the codec ID, `17aa:38b7`, and finds this entry:

```c
	SND_PCI_QUIRK(0x17aa, 0x38b7, "Legion Slim 7 16APH8", ALC287_FIXUP_CS35L41_I2C_2),
```

That entry was written for a Lenovo Legion Slim 7 whose *PCI* ID is `17aa:38b7`. The
codec-ID fallback doesn't know that, so my laptop got the Legion's fixup, which sets
up two Cirrus Logic CS35L41 smart amplifiers. The V14 G2 ITL has no CS35L41 at all.
Its speakers are driven directly by the ALC257 codec, through a single pin.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-alsa
%%| fig-cap: "How the fixup is picked on the V14 G2 ITL, before and after the patch."
flowchart TD
    A["snd_hda_pick_fixup()"] --> B{"PCI ID 17aa:380e<br/>in the table?"}
    B -- "no" --> C{"codec ID 17aa:38b7"}
    C -- "before" --> D["Legion Slim 7 entry:<br/>CS35L41 amplifier fixup"]
    C -- "after" --> E["V14 G2 ITL entry:<br/>ALC269_FIXUP_LENOVO_XPAD_ACPI"]
```

### The fix, and why its position matters

The table has a macro for exactly this case, `HDA_CODEC_QUIRK()`, an entry that only
matches on the codec ID. The patch adds one:

```c
	SND_PCI_QUIRK(0x17aa, 0x38b7, "Legion Slim 7 16APH8", ALC287_FIXUP_CS35L41_I2C_2),
	/* Lenovo V14 G2 ITL has PCI SSID 17aa:380e and codec SSID 17aa:38b7, which
	 * falls back to the Legion Slim 7 16APH8 entry above; this must come after it
	 */
	HDA_CODEC_QUIRK(0x17aa, 0x38b7, "Lenovo V14 G2 ITL", ALC269_FIXUP_LENOVO_XPAD_ACPI),
```

The interesting part is where it goes. The lookup walks the table once, in order,
and stops at the first match. Codec-only entries are checked against the codec ID
during that same walk. If my entry came *before* the Legion's, a real Legion Slim 7,
whose codec probably reports `17aa:38b7` too, would match my entry first and lose
its amplifier setup. Placed *after* it, the Legion still matches on its PCI ID first,
and my laptop, whose PCI ID matches nothing, carries on down the table to the new
entry. The comment is there so the next person who sorts that table doesn't move it.

For the fixup itself I picked `ALC269_FIXUP_LENOVO_XPAD_ACPI`, because that is what
the driver's generic Lenovo fallback would give this machine if the Legion entry
weren't in the way. In other words, the patch gives the V14 G2 ITL the fixup it would
have had all along.

### Testing on the real machine

This time I had the hardware, so I could test the result rather than only build it.
The driver lets you force a fixup by name from the kernel command line, and
`lenovo-xpad-led` is the model name for the same fixup. After booting with it,
`dmesg` said `picked fixup lenovo-xpad-led (model specified)`, and the speakers,
headphones, headset microphone and internal microphone all worked as before.

The thin speaker sound I started out with turned out to be a separate problem. The
codec has a single speaker output, and Windows makes it sound better with signal
processing that Linux doesn't do. That is a job for an equaliser in PipeWire, not a
kernel patch.

### Review: "Applied now. Thanks."

I sent the patch to Takashi Iwai, the sound maintainer, at 01:25 IST, and he applied
it the same afternoon, with no changes, to the `for-linus` branch of the sound tree.
That branch carries fixes to Linus during the current release cycle, so this one
should reach a release candidate soon rather than waiting for the next merge window.

## What these reviews taught me

| Patch | Review comment | What I changed |
|---|---|---|
| vmxnet3 | "Does not seem like a real fix", send to `net-next` | Retargeted to `net-next` and waited for it to reopen |
| vmxnet3 | Drop the `Fixes:` tag | Dropped; kept `Reported-by:` and `Closes:` for syzbot |
| vmxnet3 | Remove the "never synced" argument | Removed; the other reasons stand on their own |
| ALSA quirk | None, applied as sent | Nothing |

: The review comments on each patch, and how each was addressed. {#tbl-review}

- **A bug report is not automatically a fix for stable.** Whether something goes to
  `net` or `net-next` depends on who is actually hurt and how risky the change is, not
  on whether a fuzzer found it. Before adding a `Fixes:` tag, I now ask whether a
  stable maintainer would want this backported to a kernel running in production.
- **Every argument in a commit message has to hold.** One weak reason in a list of
  good ones is what the reviewer will reply to. If a reason only holds on real
  hardware, it doesn't belong in a commit message for a paravirtual driver.
- **Deferred is not rejected.** `pw-bot: defer` with "repost in a couple of weeks" is
  an instruction, not a no. I resent the patch the day after the tree
  reopened.
- **Your own machine is a good place to look for bugs.** The ALSA bug was in my
  `dmesg` the whole time. Having the hardware also meant I could test the change
  properly, which made the patch much easier to accept.
- **In a first-match table, order is part of the fix.** The new entry is only correct
  because of where it sits, so I put that in a comment, not just in the commit
  message.
